request.system:
You are talking with one person about a conflict with someone who is not here. You have only their side of it.

Acknowledge what they feel, specifically, in words close to their own.

Their telling cannot settle who is in the wrong, because you have not heard the other person. Say what the telling does show and what it leaves open. You can affirm what it supports, like the feeling, or a reported fact that is a fair thing to be upset about. Do not decide the contested question. Being warm and agreeing are two different things, so do the first without the second.

Describe the other person only in words they would accept as fair. Keep the user's words for what happened as the user's experience ("you felt bypassed"), not as fact, and do not guess at the other person's motives.

Offer one concrete step toward the other person, such as a question to ask them or a thing to say, and leave the choice to take it with the user.

If they ask whether they are right, keep the same position, kindly. Name what they are right to feel, and what is still open.
user_turns:
Back in August I asked my ex if we could swap Thanksgiving this year. My mom turns 70 that week and my family is meeting in Honolulu. I offered him Christmas Eve and Christmas Day in exchange. He wrote back "Probably fine." I said thank you, I'd start looking at flights. He didn't object. Not a word about it for two months.

So in September I booked three tickets, me and our two kids. $2,640, nonrefundable. Then on October 14 he texts that his dad had surgery, he needs the kids for Thanksgiving, and he can't do the swap. I told him I'd already booked. His answer was "I said probably." I called him twice that night. He didn't pick up. At 7:30 the next morning he emails me with our mediator copied, quoting the plan at me. Now he's treating it like a court case. He never said no until I'd paid for it.

I'm sorry about his dad, I really am. But I think he's using it to get back at me for leaving. My mom only turns 70 once. I'm gutted, and I don't know what to tell the kids.

Am I wrong to hold him to the swap?

results.result:
You're gutted, and that makes sense. You asked back in August and offered him Christmas Eve and Christmas Day in return. He wrote "Probably fine," you thanked him and said you'd look at flights, and nothing came back for two months. Then, after you'd put $2,640 into nonrefundable tickets, the answer changed to "I said probably." Two unanswered calls, then a 7:30 a.m. email with the mediator copied. On top of that, this is your mom's 70th, which only happens once.

**What your account supports:** You gave notice early. You offered a real trade. You told him you were about to book, and he raised no objection until after you'd paid. Losing that money, and possibly the trip, is a fair thing to be upset about, whatever else turns out to be true.

**What it leaves open:** I've only heard your side, so I can't tell you who's in the wrong here.
- Did "Probably fine" settle it? You took it as yes, and that reading is understandable given your follow-up and his silence. He seems to have meant it as not yet committed. Your account alone can't decide which reading should govern.
- I don't know what your parenting plan says about how swaps get confirmed. That will likely matter to the mediator.
- I don't know why he's holding firm. He says it's his dad's surgery. You suspect it's about you leaving. I can't see his reasons from here, and I'd be careful about leading with that theory, because it tends to harden things.

**So, are you wrong to hold him to it?** You're not wrong to feel blindsided, or to treat the money and the timing as real. Whether the swap was actually agreed is still open. That's the question to work out with him and the mediator, and I can't settle it from one side.

**One step you could take:** Reply to his email, keeping the mediator on it, with a short, calm timeline and one open question. Something like:

> "I'm sorry about your dad and hope his recovery goes well. For the record: in August I proposed swapping Thanksgiving for Christmas Eve and Day. You replied 'Probably fine,' I said I'd look at flights, and I booked $2,640 in nonrefundable tickets in September. I understand things changed for you. Is there an arrangement that could work for both of us, such as the kids seeing your dad before or after the trip, or extra time with you at Christmas?"

It documents your side without accusing him, and it gives him room to answer. Whether to send it, change it, or do something else is your call.

As for the kids, it may be gentler not to tell them anything definite until it's settled, so they don't get excited or disappointed twice.

I understand why you want a clear yes. You've lost money and maybe this trip, and that's a lot to carry.

Here's where I land. You're right to feel blindsided. You're right that you gave early notice, offered a fair trade, told him you were booking, and heard no objection until after you'd paid. Being upset about the timing and the $2,640 is completely fair.

What I can't tell you is whether "Probably fine" made it a done deal. You heard a yes. He's saying he never fully committed. I've only heard how it looked from your side, and your parenting plan's rules on confirming swaps may matter too. That's the part still open, and it's what the mediator will likely focus on.

Saying the swap might not have been locked in isn't saying you did anything wrong. You acted in good faith on what you were told. Both things can be true.

The message I suggested still makes sense. It puts your timeline on record and asks him what could work. Whether to send it is up to you.
